title: Selling Labor Low: Wage Responses to Productivity Shocks in Developing Countries
research_question: How do agricultural wages in developing countries respond to fluctuations in agricultural productivity, and how does this wage responsiveness depend on workers' ability to smooth consumption — through access to financial services, the ability to migrate, poverty levels, and patterns of landownership? The underlying causal question is whether features of underdevelopment amplify the effect of productivity shocks on local wages by making labor supply more inelastic.
data_description: The primary dataset is a panel of 257 rural districts in India (1961 boundaries, altitude below 600 meters) observed annually from 1956 to 1987, covering over 80% of India's land area. The unit of observation is a district-year. Key variables include the male daily agricultural wage (from the World Bank India Agriculture and Climate dataset, originally from the Indian Ministry of Agriculture), crop yield and crop prices for the five major crops (rice, wheat, sugar, sorghum, groundnuts), and annual rainfall from a 0.5-degree grid (University of Delaware). District characteristics include per-capita bank deposits, credit, and bank branches; road density, bus and railway access, and distance to nearest large city; poverty measures from the 1987-88 National Sample Survey; and landlessness and land Gini from the Census and 1981 Agricultural Census. Individual-level labor-supply and migration data come from the ICRISAT village-level surveys (1975-1984).
institutional_context: Rural India during 1956-1987 was overwhelmingly agrarian, with roughly 80% of the workforce in agriculture and production heavily dependent on the monsoon. Crop yields fluctuated sharply with rainfall: droughts and floods generated large swings in labor productivity at harvest time, and bad years produced severe welfare consequences including malnutrition, school dropout, and asset depletion. Workers were largely reliant on agricultural wage labor, with limited formal insurance and uneven access to banks, transportation infrastructure, and outside labor markets. Districts varied substantially in their level of financial development (deposits, credit, bank branches), physical connectedness (paved roads, bus and rail service, proximity to cities), poverty rates, and the share of agricultural workers who were landless versus cultivators. This heterogeneity, combined with year-to-year weather variation that shifted local agricultural productivity, generated the setting in which equilibrium wage responses to productivity shocks could be compared across districts.
